Aminu Masari, chairman of the Fund’s Board of Trustees, disclosed this in Abuja at the 2026 National Board of Trustees Town Hall Meeting, themed “Investing in Nigeria’s Future: Tertiary Education, Human Capital and National Development.” The allocation sits alongside other interventions, including support for Innovation and Entrepreneurship Centres and N48 billion approved for upgrading engineering and technology facilities in 12 universities. Masari said the programmes were designed to close the gap between theoretical knowledge and workplace skills, while preparing students to pursue entrepreneurial opportunities. According to him, TETFund has backed skills development in polytechnics for the past four years, picking two institutions from each of the six geopolitical zones annually. The interventions cover the establishment of skills development centres, the supply of training equipment and consumables, and capacity building for quality assurance assessors. “Nearly 1,000 assessors have been trained, with further training underway,” Masari said. He added that the programme was strengthening collaboration between polytechnics, host communities and artisans in the informal sector, giving artisans access to structured training, quality assurance mechanisms and recognised certification. This could improve their technical competence and employment prospects. Beyond skills acquisition, Masari said the Fund had approved N6.09 billion for 174 successful proposals under the 2025 National Research Fund grant cycle. The grants will support research into national challenges, particularly in science, technology, healthcare and agriculture. TETFund is also making arrangements to establish and equip six central multipurpose laboratories across the geopolitical zones to expand research capacity and access to specialised facilities. Masari further disclosed that presidential approval had been secured for six additional Centres of Excellence focused on emerging technologies, including robotics, coding, artificial intelligence, machine learning and cybersecurity. “When established, these will bring the number of TETFund-supported Centres of Excellence to 36,” he said. He noted that the Fund’s work also spans academic staff development, digital learning and renewable energy, aimed at improving teaching, research and learning conditions in beneficiary institutions. Masari cautioned, however, that higher funding for tertiary education must be matched by accountability, efficient resource management and measurable gains in educational outcomes. “The substantial increase in TETFund funding under President Tinubu places an equally substantial responsibility on the Fund and beneficiary institutions to deliver measurable improvements,” he said. He stressed that the investments would ultimately be judged by their effect on education quality, research output and graduates’ ability to contribute meaningfully to the economy. The chairman urged beneficiary institutions to properly manage and maintain TETFund-funded projects to ensure their sustainability. He also called on host communities to help secure educational institutions, protect public assets and foster an environment conducive to teaching, learning and research. Describing the town hall as a platform for stakeholders to share experiences, raise concerns and offer practical recommendations, Masari said: “I encourage frank, constructive and practical contributions. The purpose is to improve our work and ensure that public investment produces lasting benefits for Nigerians.” Reaffirming the Fund’s commitment, he added: “Investing in Nigeria’s future means equipping our people to build it.
